A patient's self-reported health-related quality of life (HRQOL) can provide independent prognostic information for survival in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. The results from various healthcare Q&A matches suggest that HRQOL data collected during routine clinical practice can help predict patient outcomes.

Based on the retrieved matches, it appears that self-reported HRQOL is associated with a longer overall survival and improved functional status in NSCLC patients. Patients who reported higher HRQOL at baseline had better survival rates compared to those with lower HRQOL scores. This finding supports the importance of collecting HRQOL data as routine clinical practice.

The matches also highlight that socioeconomic status does not significantly impact HRQOL, whereas other factors such as tumour-related characteristics and treatment response do have a more substantial influence on prognosis.

Overall, these findings suggest that self-reported HRQOL is an important prognostic factor for survival in NSCLC patients.
